title: Learning timing from Professor Tull
summary: Davenport credits Professor Tull's down-left-right-up counting method for his timing; the interviewer says his teacher Manetta taught the same.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Where do you get your timing from? How do you learn timing? Well I had some very good instructors when I started out.

Now like this guy, Tull, old Professor Tull, he was a very good music teacher. He was a very good teacher. He took lessons from him too. The old Willie Humphrey. The old Willie Humphrey, yeah. I knew him. He was fine then. And I learned a lot from Alonzo Edson. See, I was teaching up there in Greenwood, but I was taking private lessons from him. Did you ever learn anything about listening to jazz musicians? Oh yeah. I learned a lot about listening to a Louis Armstrong role.
I was teaching up there in Greenwood, but I was taking private lessons from him.

Did you ever learn anything about listening to jazz musicians? Oh yeah. I learned a lot about listening to a Louis Armstrong role. About timing? Timing? No. I didn't. Who would you pick up? Well I got my timing when I first started because this music teacher I had, Professor Tull, he was strict on time. And he had an old method of counting. You know like a musician counts with a foot, one, two, one, two, three, four. But he didn't teach that way. He taught down, left, right, up. Instead of one, two, three, four, three, down, left, right, up, which is the same as one, two, three, four. So if you make a mistake on two, you know your foot was over all this.
Well that's what Monetta used to teach me. I believe it was the same. Yeah, it was the same.
All of the old professors used to teach that way. Yeah.
Well that's better. And you keep your time then. Keep your strict. That's right. You never get lost. That's right.

Because if the beat is on three, you know you're supposed to beat to your left, not to your right. Down, left, right, up. Down, left, right, up. Instead of one, two, three, four, but it's still the same. But instead of saying one, two, three, four, you say down, left, right, up. So you know where you are. You're on the third beach, your foot is to the right.
I get my heel and toe going sometimes. You can't help yourself sometimes.

But you know the reason why I think they do that, because if you're playing in a band, where there's a conductor, that's the way he directs. That's the way he conducts. You know like one, two, three, four. Yeah. Down, left, right, up.
